query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the alloying element X controls the lattice and thermal expansion mismatch at the metal/oxide interface such that when X is a strong oxide former (e.g., Al or Si), a slowly growing, coherent, protective oxide layer forms and remains adherent at temperatures above 900 °C. In contrast, when X (e.g., Mn) does not promote such a compatible oxide phase, the oxide appears unstable and is prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state produced through conventional arc-melting and homogenization heat treatment to ensure uniform microstructure.
generation.intervention: Controlled comparison of alloys with X = Al or Si versus alloys with X = Mn, ensuring all other compositional and processing parameters are kept constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation tests at ~950 °C in an oxidative atmosphere (e.g., synthetic air or controlled O2 environment) over an extended period (e.g., 100-hour exposure) to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The metal/oxide interface where a good lattice and thermal expansion match minimizes interfacial stresses, making the oxide layer coherent and slow-growing.
generation.mechanism: The intervention acts through adjusting the crystallographic and thermal compatibility between the forming oxide (e.g., Al2O3 or silica-rich mixed oxides) and the underlying alloy substrate. A strong compatibility reduces mismatched strains during thermal cycling and oxidation, thereby slowing oxide growth and preventing the build-up of internal stresses that lead to crack initiation and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al or Si will form a continuous, slow-growing, coherent and adherent oxide layer that remains stable at temperatures above 900 °C, while alloys with X = Mn will form less compatible, stress-prone oxides that crack and spall.
generation.baseline: The baseline for comparison is the performance of the alloy with X = Mn, which is expected to develop unstable oxide layers due to poorer lattice and thermal matching with the underlying substrate.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for operation in high-temperature oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C. It is limited to alloys produced in a homogeneous solid-solution state and under controlled oxidation conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the detailed interfacial defect structures and exact mismatch strain values that govern oxide coherence, and potential interactions with secondary phases in multiphase alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Si, and Mn using identical arc-melting and homogenizing treatments. Expose polished specimens of each alloy to a controlled oxidative atmosphere (synthetic air) at 950 °C for 100 hours. Characterize the oxide layers using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and adhesion tests (e.g., bend or scratch tests) to evaluate oxide layer continuity, thickness, morphology, and adhesion.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate (via cross-sectional SEM/TEM)
Lattice matching and stress analysis at the metal/oxide interface (via high-resolution TEM and XRD)
Adhesion and spallation behavior (qualitative adhesion tests and mechanical scratch tests)
Phase identification of the oxides (via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with X = Al or Si do not exhibit a more coherent, adherent, and slow-growing oxide layer compared to the Mn-containing alloy (i.e., if there is no significant improvement in oxide stability or oxide adhesion in the Al or Si cases under identical testing conditions), the hypothesis will be falsified.
